newsitem.title: SPAIN: Bos resisted peseta rise on EMU optimism - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Bos resisted peseta rise on EMU optimism - analysts.

text.p: Persistent selling by the Bank of Spain has held the peseta at more than 84.00 to the mark for the last two months and countered pressure arising from optimism over Spain's entry into the EU single currency, analysts said on Friday.

While bonds and stocks have enjoyed a bull run on the back of Euro-optimism and a wave of foreign investment, the central bank has worked hard to keep the peseta down, thus raising official foreign currency reserves in the process, they said.
"It's evident they've sold pesetas in the last few months," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
As a result, since mid-September the peseta has been locked in a narrow range between 84.00 and 84.50 per mark.
At 1430 GMT the peseta was around 84.17/19 to the mark.
"What's happened is that the Bank of Spain hasn't let it rise versus the mark," said one analyst.
Official data show that at the beginning of November foreigners held 3.97 billion pesetas worth of bonds, up from 3.5 billion pesetas at the end of 1995.

"They had to counterbalance the flow of money coming from foreign investors. If they had done nothing the peseta would be trading somewhere around 81 per mark" said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
But behind the central bank's actions lies the will to weaken the peseta yet further, he said.
"There is evidence they would like to see a weaker peseta. When Rato took office last May he said it was desirable to have a weaker peseta. And that is their aim," Lumholdt said.
Less than one month after the new centre-right government took office, Spain's Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato said he hoped interest rates would ease and reverse part of the peseta's recent rise.
That day, May 29, the peseta opened at 83.23 per mark. Only one day later it was trading above the psychological level of 84 and has remained above that point since.
"It seems they have 84 in mind as a level, and what they want is to keep the peseta's volatility pretty low. They wouldn't like to see a rise to 83 and then maybe a decline to 85," Urrutia said.
He said that at these levels the peseta is "slightly overvalued. But actual values are not that far from a fair value", of 85 per mark.
Currency reserves rose $1.46 billion in October to $57.86 billion, and have been rising steadily from $38.23 billion in December 1995.
